notes.text: They journeyed according to the commandment of the Lord, led by the pillar of cloud and fire, and yet they came to a place where there was no water for them to drink — We may be in the way of our duty, and yet meet with troubles, which Providence brings us into for the trial of our faith.

glossa.text:
*All the multitude of the children of Israel therefore setting forward,* etc. ((ORIG., hom. 11 in Exod.)) All who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution, and are assailed by enemies: and he who walks the road of this life ought always to be ready and to stand in the camp. Whence all the synagogue of the children of Israel set forward from the desert of Sin according to their camps by the word of God. There is indeed one Synagogue of the Lord. but it is divided into four camps, which are described in the book of Numbers as placed round about the tabernacle of the Lord. Do thou therefore, armed and serving in the camp of the Lord, not entangle thyself in secular business, and keep watch always in the camp of the Lord, that it may be said of thee that thou hast set forward by the word of the Lord from the desert of Sin, and comest into Raphidim. Now Sin is interpreted *temptation*; Raphidim, *soundness of judgment:* he who comes well out of temptation comes to soundness of judgment. For in the day of judgment he will be sound. Whence Apocalypse II: *To him that overcometh, I will give of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God.* He therefore comes to soundness of judgment who orders his words well in judgment.

*Sin.* Here Sin is taken specially for one station out of those five which were from the Red Sea as far as mount Sina, which Josephus describes by name. For in general that whole desert is called Sin, as also Raphidim is.

*They encamped in Raphidim. ((HIERON. de Loc. Hebr., tom. III.))* It is a place in the desert beside mount Horeb. And it is to be known that the whole wilderness as far as mount Sinai is called Sin, and that from the whole province the place of a single station also took its name, as Moab is the name both of a city and of a province. In this solitude there are five stations, Zuph, and the desert of Sin, Alus, Depheca, Raphidim. Whence it is well said that *all the multitude of the children of Israel set forward from the desert of Sin by their stations according to the word of the Lord, and they came into Raphidim.* Whence it is plain that many stations are denoted by the name of one region.

*The people therefore thirsted there,* etc. ((ORIG., ubi supra )). Another reading: *The people,* he says, *thirsted for water, and murmured against Moses.* It was enough to say that *he thirsted,* what need was there to add *water?* The addition is not superfluous. There are therefore diverse thirsts, and each man has his own. They who are good hunger and thirst after justice ((Matth. V)). Others too say: *My soul hath thirsted after thee, O God ((Psal. XLI))* . But they who are sinners suffer not the thirst of water, not the hunger of bread, but of hearing the word of God. The people therefore thirsted for water, which ought to have thirsted for justice. But God, the instructor of the simple, the master of the unwise, corrects faults and amends errors, saying to Moses that he take the rod, and strike the rock, and bring forth waters. For he wills them now to drink of the rock and to make progress, and to come to the inner mysteries. For they murmured against Moses, and therefore the Lord commands that he show them the rock whereof they may drink. For if there is anyone who, reading Moses, murmurs against him, and the law according to the letter displeases him, because in many things it seems not to hold together, Moses shows him the rock, which is Christ, that from it he may drink and repair his thirst. But this rock does not give waters unless it is struck, and when struck it brings forth fountains: for Christ, being struck and slain upon the cross, brought forth the fountains of the New Testament. Whence Zacharias VIII: *I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered.* For unless he had been struck, and blood and water had gone forth from his side, we should all suffer thirst for the word of God. Whence: *And they drank of the spiritual rock that followed them: and the rock was Christ ((I Cor. X))*.

((ISID.)) The people, thirsting for water, murmured against Moses: therefore God commands that he show them the rock whereof they may drink. But if anyone, reading Moses, murmurs against him, and the letter of the law displeases him, Moses shows him the rock, which is Christ, and leads him to it, that from it he may drink and repair his thirst.

*Go before the people,* etc. Not Moses alone leads the people to the waters, but also the elders of the people. For not the law alone announces Christ, but also the prophets and the patriarchs and all the elders by birth.

*And the rod,* etc. ((AUG., quaest. 64 in Exod.)) It is read that Aaron, not Moses, struck the river with the rod. For Moses divided the sea with that same rod, not the river. What then does this mean: *Take the rod wherewith thou didst strike the river?* Or did he perhaps call the sea a river? and is an example of this manner of speech to be sought? Or was what Aaron did rather attributed to Moses, because through Moses God commanded the things which Aaron did, and in the one was the authority, in the other the ministry? Whence: *He shall be to thee for the people, but thou to him in those things which are unto God.*
*And thou shalt strike the rock.* Christ, who was struck upon the cross by the Jews: to whom the rod came near, that is, the wood of the passion, that water might remain for the faithful.

notes.text: My law — The doctrine which I am about to deliver. 2. Parable - Weighty sentences. Dark sayings - Not that the words are hard to be understood, but the things, God's transcendent goodness, their unparallel'd ingratitude; and their stupid ignorance and insensibleness, under such excellent teachings of God's word and works, are prodigious and hard to be believed. Of old - Of things done in ancient times.

glossa.text: *Understanding.* ((AUG.)) Because these things narrated, etc., *as far as* the things that seem open are parables and riddles. *Attend.* ((CAS.)) First the Lord himself speaks, that reverence may grow. *My people,* who obey me. The mouth of God is Asaph, who spoke these things below: *How great things we have heard from the beginning.* Of the Old Testament: or, the faithful Synagogue reproaches the wicked.
*In parables.* ((AUG.)) Parables are likenesses of things. *Propositions.* Which in Greek are *problemata,* questions having something to be resolved.

*How great things.* ((CAS.)) He tells summarily what God did for the Jews: yet for men ungrateful to him, and thus, if not to them, it profits the sons nevertheless, lest they become as their fathers. ((AUG.)) First God spoke in a man, now the man himself: *How great things we have heard.* That foretold word God spoke from himself, lest his speech be despised.

notes.text: If there be therefore any consolation — In the grace of Christ. If any comfort - In the love of God. If any fellowship of the Holy Ghost; if any bowels of mercies - Resulting therefrom; any tender affection towards each other.

Think the same thing — Seeing Christ is your common Head. Having the same love - To God, your common Father. Being of one soul - Animated with the same affections and tempers, as ye have all drank ill to one spirit. Of one mind - Tenderly rejoicing and grieving together.

Do nothing through contention — Which is inconsistent with your thinking the same thing. Or vainglory - Desire of praise, which is directly opposite to the love of God. But esteem each the others better than themselves - (For every one knows more evil of himself than he can of another:) Which is a glorious fruit of the Spirit, and an admirable help to your continuing "of one soul."
Aim not every one at his own things — Only. If so, ye have not bowels of mercies.

Who being in the essential form — The incommunicable nature. Of God - From eternity, as he was afterward in the form of man; real God, as real man. Counted it no act of robbery - That is the precise meaning of the words, - no invasion of another's prerogative, but his own strict and unquestionable right. To be equal with God - the word here translated equal, occurs in the adjective form five or six times in the New Testament, Matt. xx, 12; Luke vi, 34; John v, 18; Acts xi, 17; Rev. xxi, 16. In all which places it expresses not a bare resemblance, but a real and proper equalitg. It here implies both the fulness and the supreme height of the Godhead; to which are opposed, he emptied and he humbled himself.

Yet — He was so far from tenaciously insisting upon, that he willingly relinquished, his claim. He was content to forego the glories of the Creator, and to appear in the form of a creature; nay, to be made in the likeness of the fallen creatures; and not only to share the disgrace, but to suffer the punishment, due to the meanest and vilest among them all. He emptied himself - Of that divine fulness, which he received again at his exaltation. Though he remained full, John i, 14, yet he appeared as if he had been empty; for he veiled his fulness from the sight of men and angels. Yea, he not only veiled, but, in some sense, renounced, the glory which he had before the world began. Taking - And by that very act emptying himself. The form of a servant - The form, the likeness, the fashion, though not exactly the same, are yet nearly related to each other. The form expresses something absolute; the likeness refers to other things of the same kind; the fashion respects what appears to sight and sense. Being made in the likeness of men - A real man, like other men. Hereby he took the form of a servant.

And being found in fashion as a man — A common man, without any peculiar excellence or comeliness. He humbled himself - To a still greater depth. Becoming obedient - To God, though equal with him. Even unto death - The greatest instance both of humiliation and obedience. Yea, the death of the cross - Inflicted on few but servants or slaves.

Wherefore — Because of his voluntary humiliation and obedience. He humbled himself; but God hath exalted him - So recompensing his humiliation. And hath given him - So recompensing his emptying himself. A name which is above every name - Dignity and majesty superior to every creature.

That every knee — That divine honour might be paid in every possible manner by every creature. Might bow - Either with love or trembling. Of those in heaven, earth, under the earth - That is, through the whole universe.
And every tongue — Even of his enemies. Confess that Jesus Christ is Lord - Jehovah; not now "in the form of a servant," but enthroned in the glory of God the Father.

Wherefore — Having proposed Christ's example, he exhorts them to secure the salvation which Christ has purchased. As ye have always - Hitherto. Obeyed - Both God, and me his minister. Now in my absence - When ye have not me to instruct, assist, and direct you. Work out your own salvation - Herein let every man aim at his own things. With fear and trembling - With the utmost care and diligence.

For it is God — God alone, who is with you, though I am not. That worketh in you according to his good pleasure - Not for any merit of yours. Yet his influences are not to supersede, but to encourage, our own efforts. Work out your own salvation - Here is our duty. For it is God that worketh in you - Here is our encouragement. And O, what a glorious encouragement, to have the arm of Omnipotence stretched out for our support and our succor!

glossa.text: *If there be any consolation,* etc. If you wish to have consolation in the things of Christ, that is, in the remission of sins and in the other gifts; or: if you wish to console me, *if any comfort of charity* be yours, that is, if you wish that the charity of the churches which pray and do good things for the brethren may be to you a comfort and a strengthening in your adversities. *If any fellowship of the spirit.* On account of this fellowship, they upon whom the Holy Spirit first came spoke with the tongues of all nations. *If any bowels.* That is, if you have the affection of piety toward me. I do not say compassion itself, that is, the showing forth of mercy. If these things, I say, you wish to profit you, *fulfil my joy,* that is, be humble, *of one mind,* which you will be if you have the same mind, etc.

*Nothing through contention.* Note that there had been contentions among them. *Superior,* etc. Truly this is to be esteemed, because there can be in another something hidden whereby he is superior, even if our own good, whereby we seem to be superior, be not hidden.

*Not the things that are their own.* Here he teaches how they may avoid contention and vainglory, and how they may esteem others superior, namely if they consider not their own good things, but those of others.

*For let this be your mind,* etc. As if to say: Let each one not seek his own advantage, but that of others, as Christ did. To patience and to humility I invite you. For you ought to be minded in yourselves in that which was in Christ. As Christ sought not his own things, but ours, so let us bear one another's burdens.

*Who being in the form.* He sets high things concerning Christ before all else, that those in whom there is place for abasement may not disdain to be humbled. *He thought it not robbery.* By usurping what would not be his own, as did the devil and the first man. Or, he did not judge himself to be equal to God according to his humanity, which would have been to commit robbery, that is, to presume upon what is not his own. *But he emptied himself.* The height having been shown, he adds concerning the humility.

((Aug., Ench. c. 35 et 36)). But he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, etc., *as far as* it came about that the man Christ could have no sin.

*The form of a servant.* Not losing the form of God: the form of a servant came to him, the form of God did not depart: *He emptied himself.* To empty oneself is to show oneself visible out of the greatness of his own invisibility.
*Made.* According to the form of a servant, he who was unmade according to the form of God, and also by his own *Habit.* That is, by his manner of life.
*He humbled himself,* etc. ((CHRYS.)) Of his own accord the Son obeyed the Father, not as though into a servile, etc., *as far as* that he honoured the Father most of all.
*For which cause.* The humility of Christ having been shown, which appeared chiefly in the passion; now he shows concerning his [Christ's] glory, and what and how much humility merits.

*That in the name.* Here he opens to whom the name of God has been given, to whom every creature bends the knee, that is, to God. But perhaps it might be said that the man was God by adoption, and thus Christ in part true God, in that in part he will be adoptive. But the creature does not bend the knee to an adoptive God, but to a true one. Yet it is agreed that Christ is true God, to whom the knee is bent, not adoptive.

*That the Lord,* etc. Which here certain men deny, saying: How can it come to pass that a man should be in the glory of God the Father? but if he be adoptive, a man who is God cannot be in the glory of God the Father.

*For it is God.* Not even concerning the perseverance in good itself did God will his saints to glory in their own strength, but in himself: who gives them not only such help as he gave to the first man: without which they cannot persevere if they will, but works in them also the very willing, so that, since they will not persevere unless they both can and will, both the possibility and the will of persevering may be given them by the bounty of divine grace. For so far is their will kindled by the Holy Spirit, that therefore they can because they so will: therefore they so will, because God works that they may will.

notes.text: When he was come into the temple, the chief priests came — Who thought he violated their right: and the elders of the people - Probably, members of the sanhedrim, to whom that title most properly belonged: which is the more probable, as they were the persons under whose cognizance the late action of Christ, in purging the temple, would naturally fall. These, with the chief priests, seem purposely to have appeared in a considerable company, to give the more weight to what they said, and if need were, to bear a united testimony against him. As he was teaching - Which also they supposed he had no authority to do, being neither priest, nor Levite, nor scribe. Some of the priests (though not as priests) and all the scribes were authorized teachers. By what authority dost thou these things - Publicly teach the people! And drive out those who had our commission to traffic in the outer court? Luke xx, 1; Mark xi, 27.

I will ask you one thing — Who have asked me many: The baptism, that is, the whole ministry of John, was it from heaven or from men? - By what authority did he act and teach? Did man or God give him that authority? Was it not God? But if so, the consequence was clear. For John testified that Jesus was the Christ.
Why did ye not believe him — Testifying this.
Neither tell I you — Not again, in express terms: he had often told them before, and they would not believe him.

He answered, I go, sir: but went not — Just so did the scribes and Pharisees: they professed the greatest readiness and zeal in the service of God: but it was bare profession, contradicted by all their actions.

John came in a way of righteousness — Walking in it, as well as teaching it. The publicans and harlots - The most notorious sinners were reformed, though at first they said, I will not. And ye seeing the amazing change which was wrought in them, though at first ye said, I go, sir, repented not afterward - Were no more convinced than before. O how is this scripture fulfilled at this day!

glossa.text: *I will ask,* etc. He could have refuted them openly: but he asks for this reason, that they may be condemned either by their own silence or by their own sentence, and may know of themselves by what power he does this, according to that saying: *God shall break their teeth in their mouth.*

*Neither do I tell you.* For two causes the truth is hidden, either because the hearers are not capable, whence: *I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now;* or because they are despisers, whence *Give not that which is holy to dogs.*

*A certain man had two sons, and coming,* etc. When he had made a wary answer to the priests, he at once brings in a parable, both to convict them of impiety and to teach that the kingdom of God is to be carried over to the Gentiles.

*They say to him.* In certain codices there stands, *instead of* the first, the last. For they understand the truth, but by shifting about they are unwilling to say what they think, as in the case of John's baptism.

*John in the way of justice.* The Jews, despising John, neither grasped the way of justice, nor did penance for their evil works. *But you. ((GREG.))* Because they were unwilling to answer wisdom openly, they are caught in parables.

echoes.text: Don’t be wise in your own eyes. Fear Yahweh, and depart from evil.
echoes.note: Paul's call to do nothing through conceit and to count others better than oneself coheres with the wisdom warning 'Be not wise in your own eyes,' a recurrent sapiential theme of self-abasement. Volume is faint (no shared vocabulary in WEB) and the thought is a commonplace, so this is a contested low-confidence echo of the humility tradition rather than a pointed allusion.

echoes.text: The greater you are, humble yourself the more, And you will find favor before the Lord.
echoes.note: 'The greater you are, the more you must humble yourself' supplies a Second-Temple Jewish backdrop for Paul's 'in humility each counting others better than himself.' Availability and coherence are strong (Sirach's humility ethic was widely read), but the verbal overlap is thematic rather than lexical, marking this a faint contested echo.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: 'Emptied himself, taking the form of a servant' echoes the Suffering Servant who 'poured out his soul to death' and was 'numbered with the transgressors,' the Servant's self-emptying obedience unto death. Volume is strong given the servant/slave (doulos) language plus the death motif, and recurrence is high since the hymn climaxes in an explicit Isaiah citation (45:23), grounding availability and coherence.

echoes.text: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.
echoes.note: The downward arc 'he humbled himself, becoming obedient to death' sets up the Servant who, though abased, 'shall be exalted and lifted up,' which v.9 then fulfills. The pairing of the Servant's humiliation here and exaltation in 2:9 mirrors Isa 52:13's own movement, giving strong coherence and recurrence within the hymn.

echoes.text: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.”
echoes.note: Christ 'existing in the form of God' (en morphe theou) evokes humanity made in the image/likeness of God, the foundational image-of-God text, setting up the Adam/Christ contrast that runs through the hymn. Coherence is high with Pauline image-of-God theology (cf. 2 Cor 4:4; Col 1:15), though 'form' is not the LXX 'image,' so this remains an allusion of medium volume.

echoes.text: for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”
echoes.note: That Christ 'didn't consider equality with God a thing to be grasped' is widely read as an inverse of Adam and Eve's grasping to 'be like God' at the serpent's prompting. The Adam-Christ antithesis (humility undoing the primal grasp) gives high coherence with Pauline theology; the allusion is conceptual rather than verbal, hence medium confidence and a recognized scholarly debate.

echoes.text: He was taken away by oppression and judgment; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living and stricken for the disobedience of my people?
echoes.note: 'Becoming obedient to death, yes, the death of the cross' resonates with the Servant 'cut off out of the land of the living,' the violent, undeserved death of the righteous sufferer. The echo strengthens the broader Isa 53 matrix already active in the hymn, though the specific 'death' wording is generic, keeping confidence medium.

echoes.text: With outrage and torture let us put him to the test, That we may learn his gentleness, And may prove his patience under wrong. Let us condemn him to a shameful death; For he will be visited according to his words.
echoes.note: The righteous one condemned 'to a shameful death' who tests God's claim coheres with Christ's obedient death on the cross and subsequent vindication. Wisdom 2-5 was available and shares the suffering-then-vindicated righteous pattern, but lexical overlap with Philippians is thin, so this is a faint contested echo.

echoes.text: I have sworn by myself, the word has gone out of my mouth in righteousness, and will not return, that to me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall take an oath.
echoes.note: 'That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow... and every tongue should confess' is a direct citation of 'to me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear,' a monotheistic oracle of universal homage. Volume is maximal (near-verbatim of the LXX with knee-bow and tongue-confess parallelism), and Paul redeploys the same text in Rom 14:11, giving high recurrence; the staggering move is applying YHWH's exclusive worship to Jesus.

echoes.text: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.
echoes.note: 'Therefore God also highly exalted him' answers Isa 52:13's promise that the Servant 'shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.' The Greek hyperhypsoo intensifies the LXX's verbs of exaltation, and the Servant frame from 2:7-8 makes this the climactic vindication, yielding strong coherence and volume.

echoes.text: Declare and present it. Yes, let them take counsel together. Who has shown this from ancient time? Who has declared it of old? Haven’t I, Yahweh? There is no other God besides me, a just God and a Savior; There is no one besides me.
echoes.note: The confession 'Jesus Christ is Lord' draws its monotheistic force from the surrounding oracle ('there is no God else beside me; a just God and a Savior'), the very context of the quoted 45:23. Including the immediate co-text strengthens availability and coherence, supporting the bold identification of Jesus with the one Lord.

echoes.text: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’” God said moreover to Moses, “You shall tell the children of Israel this, ‘Yahweh, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is my memorial to all generations.
echoes.note: 'The name which is above every name' evokes the divine Name revealed to Moses, the ineffable Tetragrammaton/'I AM,' which bowing and confession honor. Coherence is high since the bestowed 'name' that draws universal worship is best read as the divine Name (kyrios = YHWH), though Exodus is not verbally cited, so confidence is medium and the precise referent is debated.

echoes.text: For thus says Yahweh who created the heavens, the God who formed the earth and made it, who established it and didn’t create it a waste, who formed it to be inhabited: “I am Yahweh; and there is no other.
echoes.note: The cosmic scope 'those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth' resonates with Deutero-Isaiah's Creator who 'formed the earth' and rules all spheres, the universal-sovereignty context of the cited oracle. The three-tier cosmos language is conventional, so this is a faint contested echo bolstering the 45:23 citation's totality.

echoes.text: Serve Yahweh with fear, and rejoice with trembling.
echoes.note: 'Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling' echoes 'Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling,' the posture of reverent obedience before God's enthroned king. The phobos kai tromos pairing is a recurrent LXX idiom Paul favors (1 Cor 2:3; 2 Cor 7:15; Eph 6:5), giving coherence; the Psalm 2 royal context coheres with the Lordship theme of 2:9-11, supporting medium confidence.

echoes.text: We have been with child. We have been in pain. We gave birth, it seems, only to wind. We have not worked any deliverance in the earth; neither have the inhabitants of the world fallen.
echoes.note: 'It is God who works in you both to will and to work' faintly recalls Isaiah's confession 'we have... wrought no deliverance in the earth' apart from God, the theme that salvation is God's effective working, not human achievement. The conceptual overlap (God as the one who works salvation) is thin verbally, so this is a low-confidence contested echo.

echoes.text: He said, “Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you plan to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian?” Moses was afraid, and said, “Surely this thing is known.”
echoes.note: The challenge 'By what authority do you do these things? Who gave you this authority?' (21:23) faintly recalls the recurring biblical motif of authority contested ('Who made you a ruler and a judge over us?'), the leader's commission questioned by his own people.

echoes.text: They assembled themselves together against Moses and against Aaron, and said to them, “You take too much on yourself, since all the congregation are holy, everyone of them, and Yahweh is among them! Why do you lift yourselves up above Yahweh’s assembly?”
echoes.note: Korah's challenge to Moses and Aaron, 'Why do you lift yourselves up above the assembly?,' is a paradigmatic disputing of divinely given authority, distantly resonant with the priests' interrogation.

echoes.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]
echoes.note: The father's command 'go work today in my vineyard' (21:28) uses the standing prophetic image of the vineyard as Israel and its work as covenant obedience, preparing for the explicit vineyard parable that follows.

echoes.text: But if the wicked turn from all his sins that he has committed, and keep all my statutes, and do that which is lawful and right, he shall surely live, he shall not die. None of his transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him: in his righteousness that he has done he shall live. Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked? says the Lord Yahweh; and not rather that he should return from his way, and live? But when the righteous […]
echoes.note: The contrast between the son who says no but repents and obeys, and the son who professes obedience but does not act, dramatizes Ezekiel's teaching that the wicked who turns shall live and the righteous who turns away shall die — repentance, not initial profession, is decisive.

echoes.text: I walk in the way of righteousness, in the midst of the paths of justice;
echoes.note: 'John came to you in the way of righteousness' (21:32) employs the Wisdom/sapiential idiom 'the way of righteousness' (cf. Prov 12:28; 21:16) for the path of life that the hearers refused.

doctrine.title: Nicene Creed
doctrine.article: the life of the world to come

notes.text: The land of Israel — The two tribes, not the ten. The fathers - Our fore-fathers. Have eaten - Have sinned. The childrens - We their children, who were unborn, suffer for their sins.

Behold — There can be no colour of partial judgment in the proceedings of God, who is equally God to all. All souls - All persons. The soul - The person, whether father or son, shall die, shall bear his own punishment.
Ashamed — Disappointed of my hope.
Cause — Without any provocation of mine.
Teach — Teach me my duty, and cause me to keep close to it, notwithstanding all temptations.
Upright — Holy and true, in all his declarations and offers of mercy to sinners. Therefore - He will not be wanting to such poor sinners as I am, but will guide them into the way of life and peace.
The meek — Such as meekly submit themselves to God, and are desirous to be directed and governed by him. Judgment - In the paths of judgment, in the right way.

glossa.text:
*Unto the end.* ((Hier.)) Here the penitent who has been scourged is set before the rest, lest they murmur in adversities: he who, having had the trial in himself, coaxes through mercy and terrifies through justice.

 *To thee, O Lord, have I lifted up.* ((AUG.)) A psalm against the adversities of the world, etc., *as far as* who not through all, the less perfect.

((CASS.)) First he asks to be taught the ways of the Lord, because he is raised up toward God.

((ID.)) Toward the contemplating of thee; he easily despises earthly things who beholds things divine.

*I trust.* ((ID.)) Having had trial of my own weakness in evils, I shall not blush because of my enemies.

*Neither let my enemies laugh at me:* and I am sure that he deceives none that endures patiently.

*In vain.* ((ID.)) Because all things are vain and unfruitful which are alien from God.

*Shew me thy ways, O Lord.* ((CASS.)) The ways are of the order of life, etc., *as far as: Direct,* belongs to life, *teach* to knowledge.

*Teach.* ((AUG.)) Truth itself, that I may understand what I believe, because I have endured; and if this suffices not: *Remember.*

*God my saviour.* ((CASS.)) There are two things which make men good, that we believe God our saviour, and that we patiently await his retribution.

*Remember.* ((ID.)) Of former sins and of those which are daily done, he prays through the mercy shewn to the ancients, and because he fears a true judge.

*Of thy tender mercies.* Compassion is properly in the shewing forth of good things.

*Which are from of old.* ((AUG.)) That is, they are from the beginning of the world: therefore let him not fail in me.

*Sins.* ((CASS.)) They are when the way of equity is forsaken.

*Of my youth.* Not for age, but for the rashness of headlong haste, which is then, when the heat of the mind exceeds moderation.

*Ignorances.* We do those things which we do not know to be evil. Or the sins of ignorance in little ones, who are held at any rate by original sin.

((HIER.)) Of my youth. Before I went out of the house of my wicked father.

*Remember me, thou.* ((AUG.)) Whose work it is to have mercy and to forgive sins.

*According to thy mercy.* That is, thy mercy is ample. Mercy is toward the wretched, goodness toward any whatsoever. But God does good both when implored by the wretched, and when led by his goodness: none is good but God.

*Sweet.* ((ID.)) Because he forgives all former things, where grace is without merits.

*Right.* Because after mercy, etc., *as far as Sweet,* because he gives sweet things; *right,* because he corrects.

*Therefore.* ((CASS.)) Because he is sweet and right; not out of cruelty, but out of kindness.

*In the way.* That is, faith, or the precepts of God. Or in the way of this life, where one must live rightly, he will give a law.

*In judgment.* While he punishes, he will direct to better things. But let them be meek who are corrected: for from wild beasts they are tamed, that they may bear it. For if they are mild, that is, of a gentle mind, as though having this by nature: he will teach them the precepts for the neglect of which came the scourges.

notes.text: If there be therefore any consolation — In the grace of Christ. If any comfort - In the love of God. If any fellowship of the Holy Ghost; if any bowels of mercies - Resulting therefrom; any tender affection towards each other.

Think the same thing — Seeing Christ is your common Head. Having the same love - To God, your common Father. Being of one soul - Animated with the same affections and tempers, as ye have all drank ill to one spirit. Of one mind - Tenderly rejoicing and grieving together.

Do nothing through contention — Which is inconsistent with your thinking the same thing. Or vainglory - Desire of praise, which is directly opposite to the love of God. But esteem each the others better than themselves - (For every one knows more evil of himself than he can of another:) Which is a glorious fruit of the Spirit, and an admirable help to your continuing "of one soul."
Aim not every one at his own things — Only. If so, ye have not bowels of mercies.

Who being in the essential form — The incommunicable nature. Of God - From eternity, as he was afterward in the form of man; real God, as real man. Counted it no act of robbery - That is the precise meaning of the words, - no invasion of another's prerogative, but his own strict and unquestionable right. To be equal with God - the word here translated equal, occurs in the adjective form five or six times in the New Testament, Matt. xx, 12; Luke vi, 34; John v, 18; Acts xi, 17; Rev. xxi, 16. In all which places it expresses not a bare resemblance, but a real and proper equalitg. It here implies both the fulness and the supreme height of the Godhead; to which are opposed, he emptied and he humbled himself.

Yet — He was so far from tenaciously insisting upon, that he willingly relinquished, his claim. He was content to forego the glories of the Creator, and to appear in the form of a creature; nay, to be made in the likeness of the fallen creatures; and not only to share the disgrace, but to suffer the punishment, due to the meanest and vilest among them all. He emptied himself - Of that divine fulness, which he received again at his exaltation. Though he remained full, John i, 14, yet he appeared as if he had been empty; for he veiled his fulness from the sight of men and angels. Yea, he not only veiled, but, in some sense, renounced, the glory which he had before the world began. Taking - And by that very act emptying himself. The form of a servant - The form, the likeness, the fashion, though not exactly the same, are yet nearly related to each other. The form expresses something absolute; the likeness refers to other things of the same kind; the fashion respects what appears to sight and sense. Being made in the likeness of men - A real man, like other men. Hereby he took the form of a servant.

And being found in fashion as a man — A common man, without any peculiar excellence or comeliness. He humbled himself - To a still greater depth. Becoming obedient - To God, though equal with him. Even unto death - The greatest instance both of humiliation and obedience. Yea, the death of the cross - Inflicted on few but servants or slaves.

Wherefore — Because of his voluntary humiliation and obedience. He humbled himself; but God hath exalted him - So recompensing his humiliation. And hath given him - So recompensing his emptying himself. A name which is above every name - Dignity and majesty superior to every creature.

That every knee — That divine honour might be paid in every possible manner by every creature. Might bow - Either with love or trembling. Of those in heaven, earth, under the earth - That is, through the whole universe.
And every tongue — Even of his enemies. Confess that Jesus Christ is Lord - Jehovah; not now "in the form of a servant," but enthroned in the glory of God the Father.

Wherefore — Having proposed Christ's example, he exhorts them to secure the salvation which Christ has purchased. As ye have always - Hitherto. Obeyed - Both God, and me his minister. Now in my absence - When ye have not me to instruct, assist, and direct you. Work out your own salvation - Herein let every man aim at his own things. With fear and trembling - With the utmost care and diligence.

For it is God — God alone, who is with you, though I am not. That worketh in you according to his good pleasure - Not for any merit of yours. Yet his influences are not to supersede, but to encourage, our own efforts. Work out your own salvation - Here is our duty. For it is God that worketh in you - Here is our encouragement. And O, what a glorious encouragement, to have the arm of Omnipotence stretched out for our support and our succor!

glossa.text: *If there be any consolation,* etc. If you wish to have consolation in the things of Christ, that is, in the remission of sins and in the other gifts; or: if you wish to console me, *if any comfort of charity* be yours, that is, if you wish that the charity of the churches which pray and do good things for the brethren may be to you a comfort and a strengthening in your adversities. *If any fellowship of the spirit.* On account of this fellowship, they upon whom the Holy Spirit first came spoke with the tongues of all nations. *If any bowels.* That is, if you have the affection of piety toward me. I do not say compassion itself, that is, the showing forth of mercy. If these things, I say, you wish to profit you, *fulfil my joy,* that is, be humble, *of one mind,* which you will be if you have the same mind, etc.

*Nothing through contention.* Note that there had been contentions among them. *Superior,* etc. Truly this is to be esteemed, because there can be in another something hidden whereby he is superior, even if our own good, whereby we seem to be superior, be not hidden.

*Not the things that are their own.* Here he teaches how they may avoid contention and vainglory, and how they may esteem others superior, namely if they consider not their own good things, but those of others.

*For let this be your mind,* etc. As if to say: Let each one not seek his own advantage, but that of others, as Christ did. To patience and to humility I invite you. For you ought to be minded in yourselves in that which was in Christ. As Christ sought not his own things, but ours, so let us bear one another's burdens.

*Who being in the form.* He sets high things concerning Christ before all else, that those in whom there is place for abasement may not disdain to be humbled. *He thought it not robbery.* By usurping what would not be his own, as did the devil and the first man. Or, he did not judge himself to be equal to God according to his humanity, which would have been to commit robbery, that is, to presume upon what is not his own. *But he emptied himself.* The height having been shown, he adds concerning the humility.

((Aug., Ench. c. 35 et 36)). But he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, etc., *as far as* it came about that the man Christ could have no sin.

*The form of a servant.* Not losing the form of God: the form of a servant came to him, the form of God did not depart: *He emptied himself.* To empty oneself is to show oneself visible out of the greatness of his own invisibility.
*Made.* According to the form of a servant, he who was unmade according to the form of God, and also by his own *Habit.* That is, by his manner of life.
*He humbled himself,* etc. ((CHRYS.)) Of his own accord the Son obeyed the Father, not as though into a servile, etc., *as far as* that he honoured the Father most of all.
*For which cause.* The humility of Christ having been shown, which appeared chiefly in the passion; now he shows concerning his [Christ's] glory, and what and how much humility merits.

*That in the name.* Here he opens to whom the name of God has been given, to whom every creature bends the knee, that is, to God. But perhaps it might be said that the man was God by adoption, and thus Christ in part true God, in that in part he will be adoptive. But the creature does not bend the knee to an adoptive God, but to a true one. Yet it is agreed that Christ is true God, to whom the knee is bent, not adoptive.

*That the Lord,* etc. Which here certain men deny, saying: How can it come to pass that a man should be in the glory of God the Father? but if he be adoptive, a man who is God cannot be in the glory of God the Father.

*For it is God.* Not even concerning the perseverance in good itself did God will his saints to glory in their own strength, but in himself: who gives them not only such help as he gave to the first man: without which they cannot persevere if they will, but works in them also the very willing, so that, since they will not persevere unless they both can and will, both the possibility and the will of persevering may be given them by the bounty of divine grace. For so far is their will kindled by the Holy Spirit, that therefore they can because they so will: therefore they so will, because God works that they may will.

notes.text: When he was come into the temple, the chief priests came — Who thought he violated their right: and the elders of the people - Probably, members of the sanhedrim, to whom that title most properly belonged: which is the more probable, as they were the persons under whose cognizance the late action of Christ, in purging the temple, would naturally fall. These, with the chief priests, seem purposely to have appeared in a considerable company, to give the more weight to what they said, and if need were, to bear a united testimony against him. As he was teaching - Which also they supposed he had no authority to do, being neither priest, nor Levite, nor scribe. Some of the priests (though not as priests) and all the scribes were authorized teachers. By what authority dost thou these things - Publicly teach the people! And drive out those who had our commission to traffic in the outer court? Luke xx, 1; Mark xi, 27.

I will ask you one thing — Who have asked me many: The baptism, that is, the whole ministry of John, was it from heaven or from men? - By what authority did he act and teach? Did man or God give him that authority? Was it not God? But if so, the consequence was clear. For John testified that Jesus was the Christ.
Why did ye not believe him — Testifying this.
Neither tell I you — Not again, in express terms: he had often told them before, and they would not believe him.

He answered, I go, sir: but went not — Just so did the scribes and Pharisees: they professed the greatest readiness and zeal in the service of God: but it was bare profession, contradicted by all their actions.

John came in a way of righteousness — Walking in it, as well as teaching it. The publicans and harlots - The most notorious sinners were reformed, though at first they said, I will not. And ye seeing the amazing change which was wrought in them, though at first ye said, I go, sir, repented not afterward - Were no more convinced than before. O how is this scripture fulfilled at this day!

glossa.text: *I will ask,* etc. He could have refuted them openly: but he asks for this reason, that they may be condemned either by their own silence or by their own sentence, and may know of themselves by what power he does this, according to that saying: *God shall break their teeth in their mouth.*

*Neither do I tell you.* For two causes the truth is hidden, either because the hearers are not capable, whence: *I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now;* or because they are despisers, whence *Give not that which is holy to dogs.*

*A certain man had two sons, and coming,* etc. When he had made a wary answer to the priests, he at once brings in a parable, both to convict them of impiety and to teach that the kingdom of God is to be carried over to the Gentiles.

*They say to him.* In certain codices there stands, *instead of* the first, the last. For they understand the truth, but by shifting about they are unwilling to say what they think, as in the case of John's baptism.

*John in the way of justice.* The Jews, despising John, neither grasped the way of justice, nor did penance for their evil works. *But you. ((GREG.))* Because they were unwilling to answer wisdom openly, they are caught in parables.

echoes.text: Don’t be wise in your own eyes. Fear Yahweh, and depart from evil.
echoes.note: Paul's call to do nothing through conceit and to count others better than oneself coheres with the wisdom warning 'Be not wise in your own eyes,' a recurrent sapiential theme of self-abasement. Volume is faint (no shared vocabulary in WEB) and the thought is a commonplace, so this is a contested low-confidence echo of the humility tradition rather than a pointed allusion.

echoes.text: The greater you are, humble yourself the more, And you will find favor before the Lord.
echoes.note: 'The greater you are, the more you must humble yourself' supplies a Second-Temple Jewish backdrop for Paul's 'in humility each counting others better than himself.' Availability and coherence are strong (Sirach's humility ethic was widely read), but the verbal overlap is thematic rather than lexical, marking this a faint contested echo.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: 'Emptied himself, taking the form of a servant' echoes the Suffering Servant who 'poured out his soul to death' and was 'numbered with the transgressors,' the Servant's self-emptying obedience unto death. Volume is strong given the servant/slave (doulos) language plus the death motif, and recurrence is high since the hymn climaxes in an explicit Isaiah citation (45:23), grounding availability and coherence.

echoes.text: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.
echoes.note: The downward arc 'he humbled himself, becoming obedient to death' sets up the Servant who, though abased, 'shall be exalted and lifted up,' which v.9 then fulfills. The pairing of the Servant's humiliation here and exaltation in 2:9 mirrors Isa 52:13's own movement, giving strong coherence and recurrence within the hymn.

echoes.text: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.”
echoes.note: Christ 'existing in the form of God' (en morphe theou) evokes humanity made in the image/likeness of God, the foundational image-of-God text, setting up the Adam/Christ contrast that runs through the hymn. Coherence is high with Pauline image-of-God theology (cf. 2 Cor 4:4; Col 1:15), though 'form' is not the LXX 'image,' so this remains an allusion of medium volume.

echoes.text: for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”
echoes.note: That Christ 'didn't consider equality with God a thing to be grasped' is widely read as an inverse of Adam and Eve's grasping to 'be like God' at the serpent's prompting. The Adam-Christ antithesis (humility undoing the primal grasp) gives high coherence with Pauline theology; the allusion is conceptual rather than verbal, hence medium confidence and a recognized scholarly debate.

echoes.text: He was taken away by oppression and judgment; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living and stricken for the disobedience of my people?
echoes.note: 'Becoming obedient to death, yes, the death of the cross' resonates with the Servant 'cut off out of the land of the living,' the violent, undeserved death of the righteous sufferer. The echo strengthens the broader Isa 53 matrix already active in the hymn, though the specific 'death' wording is generic, keeping confidence medium.

echoes.text: With outrage and torture let us put him to the test, That we may learn his gentleness, And may prove his patience under wrong. Let us condemn him to a shameful death; For he will be visited according to his words.
echoes.note: The righteous one condemned 'to a shameful death' who tests God's claim coheres with Christ's obedient death on the cross and subsequent vindication. Wisdom 2-5 was available and shares the suffering-then-vindicated righteous pattern, but lexical overlap with Philippians is thin, so this is a faint contested echo.

echoes.text: I have sworn by myself, the word has gone out of my mouth in righteousness, and will not return, that to me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall take an oath.
echoes.note: 'That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow... and every tongue should confess' is a direct citation of 'to me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear,' a monotheistic oracle of universal homage. Volume is maximal (near-verbatim of the LXX with knee-bow and tongue-confess parallelism), and Paul redeploys the same text in Rom 14:11, giving high recurrence; the staggering move is applying YHWH's exclusive worship to Jesus.

echoes.text: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.
echoes.note: 'Therefore God also highly exalted him' answers Isa 52:13's promise that the Servant 'shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.' The Greek hyperhypsoo intensifies the LXX's verbs of exaltation, and the Servant frame from 2:7-8 makes this the climactic vindication, yielding strong coherence and volume.

echoes.text: Declare and present it. Yes, let them take counsel together. Who has shown this from ancient time? Who has declared it of old? Haven’t I, Yahweh? There is no other God besides me, a just God and a Savior; There is no one besides me.
echoes.note: The confession 'Jesus Christ is Lord' draws its monotheistic force from the surrounding oracle ('there is no God else beside me; a just God and a Savior'), the very context of the quoted 45:23. Including the immediate co-text strengthens availability and coherence, supporting the bold identification of Jesus with the one Lord.

echoes.text: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’” God said moreover to Moses, “You shall tell the children of Israel this, ‘Yahweh, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is my memorial to all generations.
echoes.note: 'The name which is above every name' evokes the divine Name revealed to Moses, the ineffable Tetragrammaton/'I AM,' which bowing and confession honor. Coherence is high since the bestowed 'name' that draws universal worship is best read as the divine Name (kyrios = YHWH), though Exodus is not verbally cited, so confidence is medium and the precise referent is debated.

echoes.text: For thus says Yahweh who created the heavens, the God who formed the earth and made it, who established it and didn’t create it a waste, who formed it to be inhabited: “I am Yahweh; and there is no other.
echoes.note: The cosmic scope 'those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth' resonates with Deutero-Isaiah's Creator who 'formed the earth' and rules all spheres, the universal-sovereignty context of the cited oracle. The three-tier cosmos language is conventional, so this is a faint contested echo bolstering the 45:23 citation's totality.

echoes.text: Serve Yahweh with fear, and rejoice with trembling.
echoes.note: 'Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling' echoes 'Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling,' the posture of reverent obedience before God's enthroned king. The phobos kai tromos pairing is a recurrent LXX idiom Paul favors (1 Cor 2:3; 2 Cor 7:15; Eph 6:5), giving coherence; the Psalm 2 royal context coheres with the Lordship theme of 2:9-11, supporting medium confidence.

echoes.text: We have been with child. We have been in pain. We gave birth, it seems, only to wind. We have not worked any deliverance in the earth; neither have the inhabitants of the world fallen.
echoes.note: 'It is God who works in you both to will and to work' faintly recalls Isaiah's confession 'we have... wrought no deliverance in the earth' apart from God, the theme that salvation is God's effective working, not human achievement. The conceptual overlap (God as the one who works salvation) is thin verbally, so this is a low-confidence contested echo.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: He said, “Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you plan to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian?” Moses was afraid, and said, “Surely this thing is known.”
echoes.note: The challenge 'By what authority do you do these things? Who gave you this authority?' (21:23) faintly recalls the recurring biblical motif of authority contested ('Who made you a ruler and a judge over us?'), the leader's commission questioned by his own people.

echoes.text: They assembled themselves together against Moses and against Aaron, and said to them, “You take too much on yourself, since all the congregation are holy, everyone of them, and Yahweh is among them! Why do you lift yourselves up above Yahweh’s assembly?”
echoes.note: Korah's challenge to Moses and Aaron, 'Why do you lift yourselves up above the assembly?,' is a paradigmatic disputing of divinely given authority, distantly resonant with the priests' interrogation.

echoes.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]
echoes.note: The father's command 'go work today in my vineyard' (21:28) uses the standing prophetic image of the vineyard as Israel and its work as covenant obedience, preparing for the explicit vineyard parable that follows.

echoes.text: But if the wicked turn from all his sins that he has committed, and keep all my statutes, and do that which is lawful and right, he shall surely live, he shall not die. None of his transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him: in his righteousness that he has done he shall live. Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked? says the Lord Yahweh; and not rather that he should return from his way, and live? But when the righteous […]
echoes.note: The contrast between the son who says no but repents and obeys, and the son who professes obedience but does not act, dramatizes Ezekiel's teaching that the wicked who turns shall live and the righteous who turns away shall die — repentance, not initial profession, is decisive.

echoes.text: I walk in the way of righteousness, in the midst of the paths of justice;
echoes.note: 'John came to you in the way of righteousness' (21:32) employs the Wisdom/sapiential idiom 'the way of righteousness' (cf. Prov 12:28; 21:16) for the path of life that the hearers refused.

registers.label: Spare
lines: A father said, Go work today. One son said no, then went.
To you, O Lord, we lift our souls.
Turn, and live, says the Lord; I take no pleasure in death.
Lead us in your truth and teach us your paths.
We have said no with our lips and yes with our feet, and the other way round.
Remember not our sins; remember your mercy.
Come, let us worship the God who waits for our turning.
We come, turning toward God. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Lift your soul this morning like an offering in open hands, to the God who shows the sinner the way home.
To you, O Lord, we lift our souls.
We come like the son who said no and thought better of it, like tax collectors edging into the kingdom.
To you, O Lord, we lift our souls.
For God takes no pleasure in our dying, only in our turning; turn, and live.
To you, O Lord, we lift our souls.
Teach us your paths, lead us in your truth, and remember not the sins of our younger days.
To you, O Lord, we lift our souls.
So come, all who have turned and all who long to, and worship.
To you, O Lord, we lift our souls. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: One son said no, then turned and went to work.
We lift our souls to you.
Turn and live, says the Lord; I delight in no one's death.
We lift our souls to you.
Teach us your paths; remember not our sins.
We lift our souls to you.
Come, let us worship the God who waits.
We come, turning home. Amen.

turn.trap: Becomes generic "actions over words" moralism, detached from the specific charge — that religious leadership itself can curdle into self-protective dishonesty the instant its authority is questioned.
turn.hinge: The priests' answer about John is a calculated lie ("they reasoned with themselves... if we say...") — from the very people whose whole job is rendering honest verdicts. The story asks who is actually fit to judge, right after the judges disqualify themselves.

doors.landing: The trap of their own device
doors.claim: Jesus doesn't answer their question because they've already shown, by how they calculate their own answer, that they aren't asking in order to learn.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: The Priests revolved in their malice... For had they replied that it was from heaven, the question would follow, Why then believed ye him not?

witnesses.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: Not that they should answer it, and thereupon hear of Christ the answer to their question, but that being puzzled they should ask Him no farther.

doors.say: You can tell a question isn't honest by watching someone calculate the safest answer instead of the true one.
doors.do: Ask them to name one question they've avoided answering honestly because every true answer cost them something.

doors.landing: The son who said no, then went
doors.claim: The son who refuses and then goes is the one who actually does the father's will — promising isn't obeying, and a late yes beats an empty one.

witnesses.author: Origen
witnesses.reading: The Lord spoke to such as promise little or nothing, but in their works shine forth; and against those who promise greatly.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: The Gentile people, having done penitence, laboured in God's vineyard, and atoned by their labour for the obstinacy of the first.

doors.say: A late yes that actually shows up beats an early yes that never does.
doors.do: Have them name a commitment they said yes to quickly but haven't kept, and a "no" they later reversed with real action.

doors.claim: The ones with no religious credibility left to protect are the ones who can afford to actually change their minds — the credentialed have too much invested in already being right.

witnesses.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: I suppose that the 'publicans' here are to represent all sinful men... because avarice is found the most prevailing vice among such men.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: Others think that the parable does not relate to Gentiles and Jews, but simply to the righteous and to sinners. These by their evil deeds had rejected God.

doors.say: The people with nothing left to protect are often the first ones free enough to actually repent.
doors.do: Ask them to name what reputation or standing makes honest reconsideration costly for them personally.

semicontinuous.gravity: Israel, thirsty in the wilderness, quarrels with Moses and tests God at the rock (Exodus 17); Paul quotes the hymn of Christ who emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2); and the religious authorities demand Jesus produce his credentials, then refuse to answer his counter-question honestly because either answer traps them. The nerve: those most invested in guarding legitimate authority are the ones most willing to lie about what they actually believe, the moment truth becomes inconvenient.

synthesis.convergence: Israel, saved from Egypt, still quarrels and tests God at the rock (Exodus 17); Paul holds up Christ who emptied himself rather than grasping at status (Philippians 2); and the priests, guardians of true authority, protect their position with a lie rather than risk an honest answer. Every reading contrasts those who cling to standing with the one who let go of it — and asks which posture actually recognizes God when he shows up.
synthesis.claim: The people with the most to protect are usually the last to recognize God when he doesn't come through channels they control.
synthesis.here: For people whose credibility or track record makes honest reconsideration costly, point at the two sons — the second, later "yes" is the one that counted; a late repentance beats a protected position.

turn.subtract: Three landings — the leaders' self-trap, the late-but-real yes, or who can actually afford to repent. Choose one.
